title: How This Blog Works (and a Markdown Feature Tour)
description: A tour of every Markdown feature this site supports: code blocks, terminal output, tables, callouts, images and captions. Doubles as a reference while writing.
text: Every article on this site is a single Markdown file in the content/ directory. The build validates its frontmatter, renders it to static HTML and adds it to the archive, the tag pages, the RSS feed, the sitemap and the search index. No React code is touched to publish a post. NOTE This post is sample content that demonstrates the template. Keep it as a reference or delete it. The pipeline A post is published when it has valid frontmatter and published: true (or no published field at all). Drafts with published: false are skipped entirely, so they never reach a page, the feed or the search index. Code blocks Fenced code blocks are highlighted at build time, so no highlighting script is shipped to readers. Every block has a copy button. Terminal output works the same way, using console or text as the language: Inline code such as sudo l is styled too. Tables Field Required Example title yes "Lantern Writeup" date yes "2026 10 27" description yes 20 to 300 characters category yes writeup, research, etc. platform no HTB, THM, OffSec tags no linux, privesc Callouts TIP Write the description for someone skimming the archive. It is also used for search results and link previews. WARNING Never publish credentials, flags or details of systems you are not authorised to test. CAUTION Respect platform rules: many platforms ask that writeups of active machines stay unpublished until retirement. Headings and the table of contents Every and heading gets an anchor link and appears in the table of contents beside the article. A third level heading Use these for sub steps, such as "Enumeration → Web". Quotes Plain blockquotes stay plain, for quoting documentation or advisories.

title: JWT Algorithm Confusion: How It Happens and How to Prevent It
description: Why trusting the alg header in a JSON Web Token lets attackers forge tokens, a minimal vulnerable verifier, a demonstration, and the fix.
text: JSON Web Tokens carry their own description of how they were signed. Algorithm confusion happens when a server believes that description instead of deciding for itself. Anatomy of a token The header contains an alg field such as RS256 (RSA signature, verified with a public key) or HS256 (HMAC, verified with a shared secret). The vulnerable pattern A server verifies tokens with its RSA public key, but lets the library pick the algorithm from the token: If the library accepts both RSA and HMAC algorithms for a given key, an attacker can: 1. Obtain the server's public key (it is public, often served at /.well known/jwks.json). 2. Change the header to {"alg":"HS256"}. 3. Sign the token with HMAC, using the public key bytes as the secret. 4. The server "verifies" the HMAC with the same key bytes and accepts it. Demonstration in a lab On a deliberately vulnerable application you control: WARNING Only test systems you own or are explicitly authorised to assess. Prevention Pin accepted algorithms in code or configuration. Never use one key object for both asymmetric and symmetric verification. Reject alg: none unconditionally. Validate iss, aud and exp claims after the signature check. References RFC 7519: JSON Web Token RFC 8725: JWT Best Current Practices

title: Sample HTB Writeup: Lantern (Fictional Linux Box)
description: A template walkthrough for a fictional Easy Linux machine: virtual host discovery, a path traversal that leaks credentials, and a sudo misconfiguration.
tags: linux web path-traversal privilege-escalation sample htb
text: NOTE Sample content. "Lantern" is a fictional machine used to demonstrate the writeup layout. Replace this post with your own retired machine writeups. Summary Step Technique Foothold Path traversal in a download API User Credential reuse over SSH Root sudo tar with checkpoint action Enumeration Port scan The redirect reveals a hostname, so it goes into /etc/hosts: Virtual hosts Foothold The files vhost exposes a download endpoint that takes a filename parameter. A quick test with a relative path shows it is not normalised: The response contains /etc/passwd, which lists a svc user. Reading the application's config file leaks a database password: TIP When a file read works, check application configs, .env files and service units before going further. User The database password is reused by svc over SSH. Privilege escalation tar can execute a command at a checkpoint, a well known GTFOBins entry: Lessons Normalise and confine file paths server side; never trust a filename parameter. Unique credentials per service would have stopped the pivot to SSH. Audit sudo rules for binaries with known escape behaviour.

title: A Practical Nmap Workflow for Lab Machines
description: A fast two-stage Nmap workflow for lab targets: find open ports quickly, then run detailed scripts only where it matters, with notes on what each flag does.
text: Scanning every port with full scripts is slow. A two stage approach is faster and gives cleaner notes. IMPORTANT Scan only systems you own or are authorised to test, such as lab environments. Stage 1: find open ports Stage 2: detail on open ports only Flag reference Flag Meaning p Scan all 65535 TCP ports min rate Send at least this many packets/second sC Run Nmap's default scripts sV Probe service versions oN Save normal output to a file sU top ports 20 Quick check of common UDP ports Reading the output A redirect to a hostname is a cue to add an /etc/hosts entry and look for virtual hosts. NOTE High scan rates can miss ports on unreliable networks. If results look incomplete, rescan at a lower rate.

title: Sample THM Writeup: A Login Form and Union-Based SQL Injection
description: A template for a TryHackMe room writeup, walking through authentication bypass and UNION-based SQL injection against a deliberately vulnerable login.
text: NOTE Sample content. This is an illustrative walkthrough of a generic vulnerable login, not a record of a specific room. Replace it with your own notes. Task overview The target is a login form backed by a SQL database. The goals are to bypass authentication and then extract data from another table. Authentication bypass The server builds its query by concatenating user input: Submitting admin' as the username comments out the password check: UNION based extraction First find the number of columns with ORDER BY, increasing until the page errors: Then identify which columns are reflected and read from information schema: The fix Use parameterised queries so input is never parsed as SQL: IMPORTANT Escaping quotes by hand is not a fix. Parameterised queries are.

title: Sample OffSec Notes: A Repeatable Enumeration Methodology
description: A template for OffSec lab study notes: a structured enumeration checklist, note-taking layout and time-boxing rules that keep lab work organised.
text: NOTE Sample content. These notes describe a generic methodology and make no claims about any certification or exam. Replace them with your own. Why a methodology When a box is not giving up a foothold, the usual cause is skipped enumeration, not missing exploits. A checklist turns "stuck" into "next item". Note layout Enumeration checklist Phase Questions Network All TCP ports? Top UDP ports? Any odd service banners? Web Virtual hosts? Hidden paths? Parameters? Tech stack? Services Anonymous or default access? Version specific issues? Host Users, sudo rules, cron, SUID, writable paths? Time boxing TIP Set a timer for each rabbit hole. When it fires, write one line about what you learned and return to the checklist. 1. Spend 20 minutes on any single idea before re evaluating. 2. Re run a full port scan if nothing fits. 3. Re read your notes from the top before searching for new techniques.

title: Linux Privilege Escalation Checklist
description: A short, ordered checklist for local privilege escalation enumeration on Linux lab machines: sudo, SUID binaries, cron, capabilities and writable paths.
text: An ordered list of quick checks to run on a Linux box after getting a shell. Start cheap and local before reaching for automated tools. Identity and sudo Any NOPASSWD entry deserves a look at GTFOBins. SUID binaries and capabilities Scheduled tasks Look for scripts that run as root but are writable by your user. Writable paths and credentials TIP Note what you checked and the result. Negative results are just as useful when you come back later. Quick reference Area Command Kernel uname a Listening ss tulpn Processes ps aux Environment env

title: Sample Project: A Small Recon Notes Helper
description: A template for a personal-project post: the problem, the design, a short script that creates a per-target notes directory, and what to improve next.
text: NOTE Sample content. This describes a small illustrative script, not a released tool. Replace it with your own projects. The problem Every lab target needs the same directory skeleton. Creating it by hand is a small tax that adds up, and inconsistent layouts make older notes hard to find. The script Design choices Plain files and Bash: nothing to install on a fresh VM. set euo pipefail so typos fail loudly. No network access: the script only creates local files. Next steps 1. Add an optional first pass scan. 2. Generate a notes template per platform. 3. Add tests with bats.
